doc.title: Sonny Rollins — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Music in Harlem: records, radio, gigs
title: Music at home: Ellington, calypso, piano rolls and Fats Waller
summary: He recalls Duke Ellington, his mother's calypso records, stride piano rolls and Fats Waller, whom he loved as an early inspiration.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Okay. Um, you mentioned in your home you had recordings of Louis Jordan.
What other music was around the house? Do you have other favorite recordings other than Jordan when you were coming up?
Right. That would be the 30’s. Uh...
No, I was just going to say Duke Ellington was also a big uh uh, player. I remember my brother coming home, and uh, you know, oh, he was so excited about uh

[scatting melody of I Let A Song Go Out Of My Heart] I Let A Song Go Out Of My Heart, and all this stuff. And uh, so, we liked Duke Ellington, uh...uh, my mother had calypso records, you know. So, I heard calypso records. Um...I heard stride piano records, because in those days we always had a piano, but they had these piano rolls, you know. So, all the pianos had rolls, and these rolls were generally by people like James P. Johnson, you know, piano rolls, and uh, that was ubiquitous. And in those days there were a lot of people that were losing their apartments because of the economic situation. I think they called it “The Great Depression.” And there were always pianos out on the street from people whose, who had to move–evicted from non-payment of rent. So, there were always when you’d go walk down the street, here’s a piano, there’s somebody who’s evicted. And uh, all these pianos had rolls. They all were rolled, you know, piano rolls. So, I heard a lot of that, and I loved that. Fats Waller, in fact, was sort of one of my earliest people that I remember.
What did you like about Fats Waller?

Well, he had such a ebullience-y about him, and everything was so...like sunshine when he, you know, but his playing, I mean it was just...it, I mean, he, he wrapped the whole thing up for me. I said, I knew I wanted to play jazz. I knew that jazz was something which was good, you see, which is a theme which I sort of try to reiterate all the time. Jazz is good. It’s not just, uh...uh, it’s lecture music, it’s not uh uh, you know music, shake your booty music, and all that stuff. It has, it, it’s everything. It has everything to it, and it’s a positive. It doesn’t make you feel like fighting. It makes you feel that there is a God, and that things are okay, see. And that’s, so, I’ve always, uh–he was one of the first, he was the guy that, sort of...woke that up in me at an early age. And uh...
